sections.normalized_html: Evaluate [MATH: \displaystyle \int\limits_{C} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r},] where [MATH: \mathbf F(x, y) =(1-y)^2\,\mathbf{i} + x\,\mathbf{j}] and [MATH: C] is the line segment traversed from the point [MATH: A(0, 2)] to the point [MATH: B(1,0).]
sections.readable_text: Evaluate [MATH: \displaystyle \int\limits_{C} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r},] where [MATH: \mathbf F(x, y) =(1-y)^2\,\mathbf{i} + x\,\mathbf{j}] and [MATH: C] is the line segment traversed from the point [MATH: A(0, 2)] to the point [MATH: B(1,0).]

sections.normalized_html:
We will use the formula [MATH: \int\limits_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} = \int_a^b \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t) \,\textrm{d}t.]

First, we need to parameterize the line segment. The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are [MATH: \mathbf{a} = 2\mathbf{j}] and [MATH: \mathbf{b} = \mathbf{i}.] So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

[MATH: r(t)|= a + t(b − a); = 2j + t[i − 2j]; = ti + (2 − 2t)j,]

where [MATH: t] varies from [MATH: t=0] (at the point [MATH: A]) to [MATH: t = 1] (at the point [MATH: B]). Thus, along the curve [MATH: C,] we have [MATH: x = t, \qquad y = 2-2t.]

As a result,

[MATH: F(r(t))|= (1 − y)^{2}i + xj; = (1 − (2 − 2t))^{2}i + tj; = (2t − 1)^{2}i + tj; = (4t^{2} − 4t + 1)i + tj.]

Computing [MATH: \mathbf{r}'(t),] we get

[MATH: r^{′}(t)|= (dx)/(dt)i + (dy)/(dt)j; = (d)/(dt)(t)i + (d)/(dt)(2 − 2t)j; = i − 2j.]

Therefore, [MATH: F(r(t)) ⋅ r^{′}(t)|= ((4t^{2} − 4t + 1)i + tj) ⋅ (i − 2j); = (4t^{2} − 4t + 1) ⋅ (1) + (t) ⋅ (− 2); = 4t^{2} − 6t + 1.]

Finally, we evaluate the integral, as follows:

[MATH: ∫_(C)F ⋅ dr|= ∫_{0}^{1}F(r(t)) ⋅ r^{′}(t)dt; = ∫_{0}^{1}4t^{2} − 6t + 1dt; = ((4)/(3)t^{3} − 3t^{2} + t)|_{0}^{1}; = ((4)/(3) − 3 + 1) − 0; = − (2)/(3)]

sections.normalized_html:
We will use the formula [MATH: \int\limits_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} = \int_a^b \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t) \,\textrm{d}t.]

First, we need to parameterize the curve. Making [MATH: x] the subject of the equation, we have

[MATH: y^3 = x-5 \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad x = y^3 + 5.]

So, we can parametrize the curve using

[MATH: r(t)|= (t^{3} + 5)i + tj, 0 ≤ t ≤ 1.]

Thus, along the curve [MATH: C,] we have [MATH: x = t^3+5, \qquad y = t.]

As a result,

[MATH: F(r(t))|= yi + xj; = ti + (t^{3} + 5)j.]

Computing [MATH: \mathbf{r}'(t),] we get

[MATH: r^{′}(t)|= (dx)/(dt)i + (dy)/(dt)j; = (d)/(dt)(t^{3} + 5)i + (d)/(dt)(t)j; = 3t^{2}i + j.]

Therefore, [MATH: F(r(t)) ⋅ r^{′}(t)|= (ti + (t^{3} + 5)j) ⋅ (3t^{2}i + j); = t ⋅ 3t^{2} + (t^{3} + 5) ⋅ 1; = 3t^{3} + t^{3} + 5; = 4t^{3} + 5.]

Finally, we evaluate the integral, as follows:

[MATH: ∫_(C)F ⋅ dr|= ∫_{0}^{1}F(r(t)) ⋅ r^{′}(t)dt; = ∫_{0}^{1}4t^{3} + 5dt; = [t^{4} + 5t]_{0}^{1}; = 1 + 5 − 0; = 6]

sections.normalized_html:
The notation [MATH: \displaystyle\oint] is used to remind us that we're dealing with a line integral over a closed curve.

We will use the formula [MATH: \oint\limits_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} = \int_a^b \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t) \,\textrm{d}t.]

First, we need to parameterize a circle of radius [MATH: 1] centered at the origin. It can be parameterized as

[MATH: \mathbf{r}(t) = \cos{t}\,\mathbf{i} + \sin{t}\,\mathbf{j}, \qquad 0 \leq t \lt 2\pi.]

So, along the curve [MATH: C,] we have [MATH: x = \cos{t}, \qquad y = \sin{t}.]

As a result,

[MATH: F(r(t))|= yi + xj = \sin ti + \cos tj.]

Computing [MATH: \mathbf{r}'(t),] we get

[MATH: r^{′}(t)|= (dx)/(dt)i + (dy)/(dt)j; = (d)/(dt)(\cos t)i + (d)/(dt)(\sin t)j; = − \sin ti + \cos tj.]

Therefore, [MATH: F(r(t)) ⋅ r^{′}(t)|= (\sin ti + \cos tj) ⋅ (− \sin ti + \cos tj); = − \sin^{2} t + \cos^{2} t; = − (1 − \cos^{2} t) + \cos^{2} t; = 2\cos^{2} t − 1; = \cos 2t.]

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

[MATH: ∮_(C)F(r) ⋅ dr|= ∫_{0}^{2π}F(r(t)) ⋅ r^{′}(t)dt; = ∫_{0}^{2π}\cos 2tdt; = [(1)/(2)\sin 2t]_{0}^{2π}; = (1)/(2)\sin 4π − (1)/(2)\sin (0); = 0.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
The line integral of a vector-valued function [MATH: \mathbf F] along a piecewise smooth curve [MATH: C] is denoted

Content:
[MATH: \int\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \textrm d\mathbf r .]

Content:
This integral represents the total work done by [MATH: \mathbf F] in moving a particle from an initial point [MATH: A] to a terminal point [MATH: B] along the curve.

Content:
If the curve can be parameterized by the function [MATH: \mathbf r(t)] for [MATH: t\in [a,b],] then we can calculate the line integral using the following formula:

Content:
[MATH: \int\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \textrm d\mathbf r= \int_a^b \mathbf F(\mathbf r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t)\,\textrm dt]

Content:
Often, the trickiest part is finding a parameterization for [MATH: C.] In this lesson, we'll consider several different cases

---

Item 2 — Example: Line Integrals Over Line Segments

Example Prompt:
Evaluate [MATH: \displaystyle \int\limits_{C} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r},] where [MATH: \mathbf F(x, y) =(1-y)^2\,\mathbf{i} + x\,\mathbf{j}] and [MATH: C] is the line segment traversed from the point [MATH: A(0, 2)] to the point [MATH: B(1,0).]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We will use the formula
[MATH: \int\limits_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} = \int_a^b \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t) \,\textrm{d}t.]

First, we need to parameterize the line segment.
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are
[MATH: \mathbf{a} = 2\mathbf{j}] and [MATH: \mathbf{b} = \mathbf{i}.]
So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

[MATH: r(t)|= a + t(b − a); = 2j + t[i − 2j]; = ti + (2 − 2t)j,]

where [MATH: t] varies from [MATH: t=0] (at the point [MATH: A]) to [MATH: t = 1] (at the point [MATH: B]).
Thus, along the curve [MATH: C,] we have
[MATH: x = t, \qquad
y = 2-2t.]

As a result,

[MATH: F(r(t))|= (1 − y)^{2}i + xj; = (1 − (2 − 2t))^{2}i + tj; = (2t − 1)^{2}i + tj; = (4t^{2} − 4t + 1)i + tj.]

Computing [MATH: \mathbf{r}'(t),] we get

[MATH: r^{′}(t)|= (dx)/(dt)i + (dy)/(dt)j; = (d)/(dt)(t)i + (d)/(dt)(2 − 2t)j; = i − 2j.]

Therefore,
[MATH: F(r(t)) ⋅ r^{′}(t)|= ((4t^{2} − 4t + 1)i + tj) ⋅ (i − 2j); = (4t^{2} − 4t + 1) ⋅ (1) + (t) ⋅ (− 2); = 4t^{2} − 6t + 1.]

Finally, we evaluate the integral, as follows:

[MATH: ∫_(C)F ⋅ dr|= ∫_{0}^{1}F(r(t)) ⋅ r^{′}(t)dt; = ∫_{0}^{1}4t^{2} − 6t + 1dt; = ((4)/(3)t^{3} − 3t^{2} + t)|_{0}^{1}; = ((4)/(3) − 3 + 1) − 0; = − (2)/(3)]

Item 5 — Example: Line Integrals Over Cartesian Curves

Example Prompt:
Evaluate [MATH: \displaystyle \int\limits_{C} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r},] where [MATH: \mathbf F(x, y) = y\,\mathbf{i} + x\,\mathbf{j}] and [MATH: C] is the curve [MATH: y^3 = x-5] traversed from the point [MATH: A(5,0)] to the point [MATH: B(6,1).]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We will use the formula
[MATH: \int\limits_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} = \int_a^b \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t) \,\textrm{d}t.]

First, we need to parameterize the curve. Making [MATH: x] the subject of the equation, we have

[MATH: y^3 = x-5
\qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad
x = y^3 + 5.]

So, we can parametrize the curve using

[MATH: r(t)|= (t^{3} + 5)i + tj, 0 ≤ t ≤ 1.]

Thus, along the curve [MATH: C,] we have
[MATH: x = t^3+5, \qquad
y = t.]

As a result,

[MATH: F(r(t))|= yi + xj; = ti + (t^{3} + 5)j.]

Computing [MATH: \mathbf{r}'(t),] we get

[MATH: r^{′}(t)|= (dx)/(dt)i + (dy)/(dt)j; = (d)/(dt)(t^{3} + 5)i + (d)/(dt)(t)j; = 3t^{2}i + j.]

Therefore,
[MATH: F(r(t)) ⋅ r^{′}(t)|= (ti + (t^{3} + 5)j) ⋅ (3t^{2}i + j); = t ⋅ 3t^{2} + (t^{3} + 5) ⋅ 1; = 3t^{3} + t^{3} + 5; = 4t^{3} + 5.]

Finally, we evaluate the integral, as follows:

[MATH: ∫_(C)F ⋅ dr|= ∫_{0}^{1}F(r(t)) ⋅ r^{′}(t)dt; = ∫_{0}^{1}4t^{3} + 5dt; = [t^{4} + 5t]_{0}^{1}; = 1 + 5 − 0; = 6]
